title: Hearing, Touch, & Pain: Auditory Transduction, Somatosensory Homunculus, & Gate Control
description: Explore cochlear hair cells, tonotopic maps, Penfield's sensory homunculus, nociceptive fibers, and the Gate Control Theory of pain.

slides.title: Auditory Transduction & Tonotopy in the Cochlea 🎵
slides.content:
# The Mechanical Symphony of Sound

1. Sound pressure waves funnel into the external auditory canal, vibrating the **tympanic membrane** (eardrum).
2. The middle ear ossicles (**malleus, incus, stapes**) amplify sound vibrations and push against the **oval window** of the fluid-filled **cochlea**.
3. Fluid displacement ripples the **basilar membrane**, shearing stereocilia on inner hair cells against the tectorial membrane.
4. Deflection of stereocilia mechanically yanks open tip links, allowing an influx of **potassium ($K^+$)** from the endolymph to depolarize the hair cell and release glutamate!

* **Tonotopic Organization**: The basilar membrane is physically tuned by stiffness:
  * **Base (Narrow & Stiff)**: Resonates to **high frequencies** (up to 20,000 Hz).
  * **Apex (Wide & Flexible)**: Resonates to **low frequencies** (down to 20 Hz).

quizData.question: Which portion of the cochlear basilar membrane vibrates maximally in response to high-frequency sounds (e.g., 15,000 Hz)?

options.text: The narrow, stiff base near the oval window
The wide, flexible apex at the helicotrema
The middle turn equally across all frequencies

quizData.explanation: High-frequency acoustic vibrations displace the stiff, narrow base of the basilar membrane near the oval window.

slides.title: The Somatosensory Homunculus & Cortical Magnification 🖐️
slides.content:
## Mapping the Body on the Brain

In the 1930s, Canadian neurosurgeon **Wilder Penfield** electrically stimulated the primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus) of awake patients undergoing epilepsy surgery, discovering an orderly topological map of the human body: the **Sensory Homunculus**.

* **Cortical Magnification**: The cortical space allocated to a body part is proportional to its **tactile receptor density** and functional importance, NOT its physical surface area!
* Hands, fingers, lips, tongue, and genitalia occupy massive cortical territory, reflecting high tactile sensitivity and two-point discrimination acuity.
* In contrast, the trunk, back, and thighs have sparse receptive fields and are represented by tiny cortical strips.

slides.title: Nociception & The Gate Control Theory of Pain 🚪
slides.content:
## Why Rubbing a Bruise Helps

Pain signals travel along two distinct primary afferent pathways:
* **A-delta ($A\delta$) Fibers**: Lightly myelinated, rapid conduction (5-30 m/s); transmit **acute, sharp, localized, stabbing pain**.
* **C Fibers**: Unmyelinated, sluggish conduction (0.5-2 m/s); transmit **slow, dull, burning, diffuse, throbbing pain**.

### Melzack & Wall's Gate Control Theory (1965):
In the dorsal horn substantia gelatinosa, inhibitory interneurons act as a physiological **'gate'** controlling whether pain signals reach ascending spinothalamic transmission cells (T-cells):
1. Nociceptive $C$ fibers *inhibit* the interneuron, opening the gate and allowing intense pain signals to travel up to the brain.
2. Non-painful mechanical touch fibers (**$A\beta$ fibers**) *activate* the inhibitory interneuron.
3. Therefore, rubbing your shin after bumping it activates $A\beta$ touch fibers, closing the gate and dampening the pain signal before it reaches consciousness!

quizData.question: According to the Gate Control Theory, how does rubbing a bumped elbow reduce perceived pain?

options.text: A-beta touch fibers excite inhibitory spinal interneurons, closing the neural gate against C-fiber pain transmission
Rubbing permanently severs the ascending spinothalamic tract
It accelerates conduction of slow C fibers so pain ends faster
It eliminates all endorphin secretion in the periaqueductal gray

quizData.explanation: Mechanical touch signals carried by large A-beta fibers stimulate inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn, closing the gate on pain projection neurons.
